frameworks.name: How Your Role Makes The Company Money
frameworks.definition: A diagnostic framework for mapping any employee's impact to revenue by identifying the cost consequences of poor performance and translating those into measurable operational standards.

claims.text: Most employees in an organization cannot answer how their role makes the company money, even when asked directly. This absence of clarity represents both a loss of meaning for the employee and a diagnostic gap for leadership.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: To map any role's revenue impact, first identify what bad performance in that role costs the business, then reverse each cost into a measurable operational standard. For example, a camera operator's poor work creates: wasted team time, lower media performance (framing issues, lighting), wasted footage, and equipment misalignment—so the measurable standards become: correct file saves, proper naming, appropriate timestamping, correct drive storage, correct camera setup, and on-time starts.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Defining performance via negative-consequence mapping forces observable, measurable criteria rather than vague interpretations of value. This makes the employee's impact tangible and verifiable.
bounded_by: Does not require the role to generate revenue directly
Applies equally to sales roles (straightforward: bringing in money) and ancillary roles (indirect cost prevention)

claims.text: When an employee understands how their work connects to company revenue—either through direct income generation or through cost prevention—it unlocks meaning and clarifies their actual impact, even if they previously felt their role was low-impact.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Employee has explicit understanding of role-to-revenue mapping
claims.mechanism: Understanding creates meaning; meaning sustains engagement. Without this clarity, employees often believe they have no impact when in fact their impact is simply invisible to them.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the impact mapping is inaccurate or the role genuinely adds no value

claims.text: The statement 'I wish I had more impact' typically reflects lack of visibility into existing impact, not an absence of impact. Most employees in their current role do have measurable impact; the constraint is awareness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Employee has not been explicitly mapped to revenue impact
Role contains measurable value-creation or cost-prevention activities
claims.mechanism: Impact exists but goes unnamed. Naming it makes it real and actionable to the employee.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the role has been accurately audited and contains no material impact

examples.text: A camera operator holds the camera. When asked how this makes the company money, the immediate answer is unclear. But examining failure modes reveals the answer: bad camera work wastes the entire team's time, degrades media performance (off-center framing, poor lighting), wastes footage, and requires misaligned equipment spending. Reversing these costs yields measurable standards: files saved correctly 100% of the time, named correctly in the system, saved to the correct drive, timestamped appropriately, camera and lighting set up correctly, and start times met. When the operator hits all five standards at 100%, they can say 'I'm making the company money, and here's exactly how.'

practices.text: Ask every employee: How do you and your role make the company money? If they cannot answer, work backwards from failure costs to define measurable operational standards for their role.
For sales roles, the answer is straightforward: bring in money. Make sure every rep can articulate the mechanism.
For ancillary roles, reverse each cost of poor performance into a measurable standard, then track compliance to that standard as the role's revenue-impact proxy.
